title: Unit 2: Force and Translational Dynamics

topics.name: Newton's laws
covers: Newton’s laws of motion: first and second law
Newton’s laws of motion: third law

guide.title: Force and translational dynamics: review guide
guide.intro: Dynamics explains motion with forces. This unit defines systems and their center of mass, applies Newton's laws (including forces that change with time or speed), and covers circular motion and gravitation.
guide.equationNote: g = 10 m/s² near Earth's surface unless a question says otherwise; G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

sections.title: Systems and center of mass
body: A system is whatever group of objects you choose to analyze together. Forces between objects inside it are internal and cancel in pairs; only external forces change the motion of its center of mass: F_ext = M·a_cm.
Center of mass: x_cm = Σmᵢxᵢ / Σmᵢ for separate objects, or x_cm = ∫x dm / ∫dm for a continuous object, where dm = λ dx for a rod with linear density λ.
points: For a uniform object, the center of mass is at its geometric center.
With no net external force, the center of mass keeps a constant velocity, even when the parts push on each other or break apart.
Choose the system to make the problem simple: treating two objects as one system hides the forces between them.
equations: center of mass of a continuous object

sections.title: Newton's laws
body: First law: with no net force, an object's velocity stays constant. Second law: F_net = ma, or more generally F_net = dp/dt. Third law: when A pushes on B, B pushes on A with an equal and opposite force; the two forces act on different objects.
Draw a free-body diagram for each object, choose axes, and write F_net = ma along each axis. Connected objects share an acceleration, and an ideal string has the same tension throughout.
points: Third-law pairs never appear on the same free-body diagram.
With a resistive force F = −bv, a falling object approaches a terminal speed where the net force is zero: mg = bv_T.
Kinetic friction is f = μ_k N; static friction can take any value up to μ_s N.
equations: f ≤ μ_s N, f = μ_k N

sections.title: Circular motion and gravitation
body: An object moving in a circle at constant speed accelerates toward the center: a_c = v²/r = ω²r. Real forces (tension, friction, gravity, the normal force) must add up to a net inward force of mv²/r.
Newton's law of gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r², attractive, with r measured between centers. For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force, so v = √(GM/r).
points: Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for the net inward force.
Gravitational field strength falls off as 1/r²: at twice the distance from Earth's center, g is one quarter as large.
On a flat curve, static friction provides the inward force: v_max = √(μ_s g r).

example.prompt: A 1200 kg car rounds a flat curve of radius 40 m at 12 m/s. What friction force is needed, and what is the smallest coefficient of static friction that allows this?
example.solution: The friction must supply the centripetal force: f = mv²/r = (1200)(12²)/40 = 4320 N. Since f ≤ μ_s mg, μ_s ≥ v²/(gr) = 144/400 = 0.36.

misconceptions: “Action and reaction cancel, so nothing can accelerate.”
They act on different objects, so they never cancel on a single object.
“Centripetal force is an extra force to draw on the diagram.”
It is the net inward force from the real forces already there.
“The tension in a string always equals the hanging weight.”
Only when the hanging object is not accelerating.
“Internal forces change the motion of the center of mass.”

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg mass is at x = 0 and a 6.0 kg mass is at x = 4.0 m. Where is their center of mass?
choiceExplanations: 2.0 m is the midpoint, which is the center of mass only for equal masses.
1.0 m puts the center of mass nearer the lighter mass, as if the masses were swapped.
24 is Σmx; it must be divided by the total mass, 8.0 kg.

questions.prompt: A thin rod lies along the x-axis from x = 0 to x = L. Its linear mass density is λ = kx, where k is a constant. Where is its center of mass?
questions.explanation: x_cm = ∫x·λ dx / ∫λ dx = ∫₀ᴸ kx² dx / ∫₀ᴸ kx dx = (kL³/3)/(kL²/2) = 2L/3. More mass is near x = L, so the center of mass shifts that way.
choiceExplanations: L/2 is correct only for a uniform rod; here the density increases along the rod.
L/3 would fit a rod whose density decreases along x, the reverse of this one.
3L/4 is the result for a density proportional to x², not to x.

questions.prompt: A projectile explodes into two pieces at the top of its path. Ignoring air resistance, what path does the center of mass of the pieces follow after the explosion, until either piece lands?
choices: The same parabola the projectile was following
A straight line downward from the explosion point
It stops moving, because the pieces fly apart in opposite directions
It depends on the masses of the pieces
questions.explanation: The explosion forces are internal, so they do not change the center of mass's motion. The only external force is still gravity, so the center of mass keeps following the original parabola.
choiceExplanations: The center of mass keeps its horizontal velocity, because no external horizontal force acts.
Internal forces cannot stop the center of mass; its velocity changes only through external forces.
The masses decide where each piece goes, but not the path of the center of mass.

questions.prompt: A net force of 12 N acts on a 3.0 kg box on a frictionless floor. What is its acceleration?
choiceExplanations: 36 multiplies force and mass; acceleration is force divided by mass.
0.25 is m/F, the ratio upside down.
15 adds the force and the mass, which have different units.

questions.prompt: A 3.0 kg block on a frictionless table is tied by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley to a hanging 2.0 kg block. What is the tension in the string? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: For the two-block system, the net force is the hanging weight, 20 N, so a = 20 ÷ 5.0 = 4.0 m/s². The string is the only horizontal force on the table block: T = (3.0)(4.0) = 12 N.
choiceExplanations: 20 N is the hanging block's weight; the tension is less because that block accelerates downward.
8.0 N is the net force on the hanging block, (2.0)(4.0), not the tension.
30 N is the weight of the block on the table, which is balanced by the normal force.

questions.prompt: A large truck collides head-on with a small car. How do the forces they exert on each other compare during the collision?
choices: They are equal in size and opposite in direction
The truck exerts the larger force
The car exerts the larger force
It depends on which one was moving faster
questions.explanation: Newton's third law: the forces two objects exert on each other are always equal in size and opposite in direction. The car accelerates more because its mass is smaller, not because it feels a bigger force.
choiceExplanations: The truck's larger mass changes its acceleration, not the size of the force pair.
Third-law forces are equal; neither object exerts more on the other.
Speed affects how large the force pair is, but the two forces are still equal to each other.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg object falls through a fluid that exerts a resistive force of magnitude bv, with b = 4.0 N·s/m. What is its acceleration when its speed is 2.5 m/s? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Net force = mg − bv = 20 N − (4.0)(2.5) N = 10 N downward, so a = 10 N ÷ 2.0 kg = 5.0 m/s². (Its terminal speed is mg/b = 5.0 m/s.)
choiceExplanations: 10 m/s² ignores the resistive force, which is 10 N at this speed.
The acceleration is zero only at the terminal speed, mg/b = 5.0 m/s, not at 2.5 m/s.
15 m/s² adds the resistive force to the weight; it opposes the downward motion.

questions.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius 2.0 m at a constant 4.0 m/s. What net force acts on it?
questions.explanation: F = mv²/r = (0.50)(4.0)²/2.0 = 4.0 N, directed toward the center of the circle.
choiceExplanations: 1.0 N is mv/r; the speed must be squared.
16 N multiplies by r instead of dividing.
2.0 is mv, the momentum, not the force.

questions.prompt: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m. The coefficient of static friction between the tires and the road is 0.80. What is the maximum speed at which it can take the curve without sliding? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Static friction supplies the centripetal force: μ_s mg = mv²/r, so v = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.80 × 10 × 50) = √400 = 20 m/s.
choiceExplanations: 22 m/s is √(gr), which leaves out the coefficient of friction.
25 m/s divides by μ_s instead of multiplying.
400 is v²; the square root is still needed.

questions.prompt: On Earth's surface, g = 9.8 m/s². What is the gravitational field strength at a height above the surface equal to Earth's radius?
questions.explanation: Field strength goes as 1/r², with r measured from Earth's center. At a height of one radius, r = 2R, so g = 9.8/2² ≈ 2.5 m/s².
choiceExplanations: 4.9 m/s² uses 1/r; gravity falls off as 1/r².
Gravity weakens with distance from Earth's center.
1.1 m/s² uses r = 3R; the distance from the center is R + R = 2R.

questions.prompt: Two satellites orbit Earth in circular orbits. Satellite B's orbital radius is four times satellite A's. How does B's orbital speed compare with A's?
questions.explanation: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). Four times the radius gives 1/√4 = 1/2 the speed.
choiceExplanations: One quarter would be true if v were proportional to 1/r; it goes as 1/√r.
A larger orbit is slower, not faster, because gravity is weaker there.
One sixteenth uses 1/r²; that is how the gravitational force changes, not the speed.
